items.prompt: Dev isn't anyone's manager and isn't on the steering committee, yet he ends up shaping which migration strategy gets picked. What kind of authority is he using?
choices: Formal authority, because he's a senior engineer
Informal authority — influence built through trust and credibility, not a title
No real authority — he just got lucky
Delegated authority from his manager
items.explanation: Formal authority comes from a title — the right to assign, approve, or decide. Dev has none of that here. What he uses instead is informal authority: influence earned through trust, credibility, and relationships, which doesn't require a title to be real.
items.reference:
Formal authority

Comes from a title: assign, approve, say yes/no

Informal authority

Comes from trust and credibility, no title needed

Why: a title isn't required to move a decision — trust and credibility do real work on their own.
items.learnMore:
Formal vs. informal authority

Every organization runs on two overlapping systems of influence, and only one of them shows up on the org chart.

Formal authorityInformal authority
SourceA title or roleTrust, credibility, relationships
Visible on org chart?YesNo
Can you build it without a promotion?NoYes

Most people who influence decisions they don't own are relying entirely on the informal kind — which means it can be deliberately built, not just waited for.

Common mistake

Assuming that without a title, nothing can be done except wait for one. Informal authority is buildable starting today, through the same trust-building moves as any other relationship.

items.prompt: Which of these is the clearest example of formal authority, as distinct from informal authority?
choices: A well-liked engineer whose opinion people tend to seek out before deciding
A director who can approve or reject a budget request, and it's final
A tech lead people trust because they're reliably right
A colleague other people go to for advice before a big decision
items.explanation: A director approving or rejecting a budget request is formal authority in its purest form — the power comes directly from the title, and the decision is final regardless of how anyone feels about the director personally. The other three examples describe informal authority: influence earned through trust and track record, with no title behind it.

items.prompt: True or false: informal authority only matters for people who don't yet have formal authority — once someone becomes a manager or director, informal authority stops being relevant.
choices: True — formal authority replaces the need for informal authority
False — even people with formal authority need informal authority to get buy-in on anything contested or cross-team
True, because formal authority can simply be ordered rather than earned
False, but only for individual contributors, never for managers
items.explanation: Formal authority doesn't make informal authority obsolete. A director can order a decision within their own reporting line, but most consequential decisions cross team boundaries, where the director has no formal power either — and needs the same trust-and-credibility-based influence anyone else would.

items.prompt: VP Farid's signature is officially required to approve the migration strategy. But Farid always signs whatever the four tech leads agree on. Who is the real decision-maker here?
choices: Farid, because his signature is legally required
The four tech leads, because their consensus is what Farid actually defers to
Nobody — the decision is made collectively with no real leverage point
Whoever presents last in the meeting
items.explanation: Farid is the nominal decision-maker — his name is on the sign-off. But he consistently defers to the tech leads' consensus rather than exercising independent judgment, which makes the four tech leads the real decision-makers. Convincing Farid alone, without reaching them, wouldn't move the actual decision.
items.reference:
🖋️ Nominal decision-maker — name on the sign-off
🧭 Real decision-maker(s) — whose input actually can't be overruled

Why: arguing to the nominal decision-maker while the real decision has already been made elsewhere is a common, avoidable failure.
items.learnMore:
Nominal vs. real decision-makers

Every decision has two maps. They usually overlap, but not always — and the gap between them is where a lot of influence attempts fail.

QuestionWhat it reveals
Whose name is on the decision?The nominal (org-chart) answer
Whose objection would actually stop it?The real answer
Do those two answers match here?If not, focus effort on the real answer

VP Farid's name is on the sign-off, but he defers to the four tech leads' consensus — which makes them the real decision-makers, even though none of them hold the sign-off title.

Common mistake

Treating the org chart as the whole map. A decision-maker who says 'what does the team think?' before deciding is telling you, out loud, who the real decision-maker actually is.

items.prompt: What's the most reliable signal that a nominal decision-maker is actually deferring to someone else's judgment?
choices: They take a long time to respond to emails
They ask 'what do you all think?' before deciding, and consistently go with the answer
They hold the highest title in the room
They speak the most during meetings
items.explanation: A decision-maker who routinely asks for the room's input before deciding — and then goes with it — is telling you directly who the real decision-maker is. Title and meeting airtime don't reveal this; the actual pattern of whose input changes the outcome does.

items.prompt: Dev is deciding when to first raise his concern with the tech leads. Which is more likely to actually change minds: raising it live in the decision meeting, or in private conversations days beforehand?
choices: Live in the meeting — a strong argument works regardless of timing
Private conversations days beforehand — people rarely change a position on the spot, in front of an audience
It makes no difference as long as the argument is correct
Live in the meeting, because it puts more pressure on people to agree
items.explanation: People rarely change a position live, in front of an audience, without time to think it over. A private conversation days before gives someone room to genuinely reconsider and arrive at the meeting already aligned — which reads as their own judgment, not a concession made under pressure.
items.reference:
During the meetingBefore the meeting
Time to reconsiderNone — on the spotDays, in private
Social pressureHigh — audience watchingLow — one-on-one
Likely outcomeDefaults to prior positionRoom to genuinely change

Why: a position rarely changes live, in front of an audience, without time to sit with it first.
items.learnMore:
Coalition timing

The same argument, made at two different times, has very different odds of changing anyone's mind.

TimingWhat happens
During the meeting, coldPeople default to their prior position; changing it live feels like losing face
Days before, privatelyRoom to actually reconsider, ask questions, and arrive already aligned

A coalition built before the decision moment changes what that moment even is — a confirmation of shared ground, not a live argument.

Common mistake

Saving the strongest version of the argument for the meeting itself, assuming a good argument works regardless of timing. Timing changes whether the argument gets a fair hearing at all.

items.prompt: Why does a coalition built 'during' the decision moment, from a standing start, almost never work?
choices: Because people are naturally stubborn and never change their minds
Because there isn't time to genuinely reconsider a position in front of an audience, on the spot
Because meetings are too short for any real discussion
Because it's against most companies' policies
items.explanation: It's not stubbornness — it's that changing a position live, in front of an audience, with no time to think, feels like losing face rather than reasoning your way to a better answer. A private conversation beforehand removes both the audience and the time pressure.

items.prompt: Dev has never interacted with Sana before. What is reciprocity, in the context of asking for her support on a contested decision?
choices: Reminding Sana of a company policy that requires her to help
Offering something genuinely useful in exchange, roughly matched in size to what's being asked
Simply being polite when making the ask
Waiting for Sana to offer help first, unprompted
items.explanation: Reciprocity is a two-way exchange — offering something real and useful, sized to roughly match what's being asked for. It's not politeness, and it's not a one-directional request dressed up as a favor.
items.reference:
🤝 Reciprocity — trading real help now for support later
⚖️ The size of the favor should roughly match the size of the ask

Why: an ask with nothing traded for it, from someone with no relationship, tends to land as one-sided.
items.learnMore:
Reciprocity as currency

An ask rarely lands as fair in isolation — it lands as fair (or doesn't) relative to what's been exchanged around it.

What it is
ReciprocityAn active, two-way exchange — offering something useful now, not cashing in old chips
SizingA small favor buys a short conversation, not public support on a contested decision

This isn't a favor bank where old chips get cashed in — it's closer to an active, ongoing exchange happening around the same time as the ask.

Common mistake

Assuming any past favor, of any size, entitles you to any future ask, of any size. The size of what's traded has to roughly match the size of what's being requested.

items.prompt: Why might a single small favor not be enough to earn someone's public support on a contested, company-wide decision?
choices: Because favors don't actually build any trust at all
Because the size of what's traded should roughly match the size of the ask, and public support on a contested decision is a large ask
Because favors only count if they're announced publicly
Because reciprocity doesn't apply to work relationships
items.explanation: A small favor and a large, public, contested ask aren't equivalent — the exchange has to roughly balance. A small favor might buy a short, honest conversation; it typically doesn't buy someone's public support on something they'd have to defend to others.

items.prompt: Dev raises his risk concern with Farid, who responds: 'You're not even on-call for order-routing — why are you worried about this?' What's the most effective next move?
choices: Repeat the argument more forcefully to prove he's serious
Drop the concern entirely since he lacks standing
Find someone whose standing on this exact topic is unquestioned, and have them make the same point
Escalate straight to Farid's manager
items.explanation: Farid's objection is about standing, not content — no amount of restating the same argument fixes a credibility gap. The effective move is a credible messenger: someone whose standing on that specific topic isn't in question, carrying the same point with more weight than Dev currently has.
items.reference:
Dev's standing

Not on-call for order-routing, never run this kind of incident

Priya's standing

SRE lead, has run 3 prior cutover incidents

Why: the same words carry different weight depending on who says them — the fix for a standing gap is a different messenger, not a louder argument.
items.learnMore:
Credible messengers

Sometimes the obstacle isn't the argument — it's who's making it.

What it addresses
More arguingDoesn't fix a standing gap — the content was never the problem
A credible messengerSomeone whose standing on that exact topic isn't in question carries the same point with more weight

A credible messenger doesn't replace the coalition-building work — they're most useful for the one piece of the case where the asker's own standing runs thin.

Common mistake

Assuming a standing gap can be closed by restating the same argument more forcefully. If the issue is who's saying it, more force on the same voice doesn't fix it.

items.prompt: What makes Priya an effective credible messenger for the migration-risk concern specifically?
choices: She agrees with Dev on everything
She has run three prior cutover incidents, giving her unquestioned standing on this exact risk
She has a more senior title than Dev
She is better at public speaking than Dev
items.explanation: A credible messenger's value comes from standing on the specific topic, not general seniority or speaking skill. Priya has directly run three prior cutover incidents — that track record is what makes the same point land differently coming from her.

items.prompt: Which opening line is more likely to persuade Sana, whose team owns order-routing and would be paged if something breaks?
choices: 'I'm worried the hard cutover is too risky'
'If something breaks during a hard cutover, you're the one paged at 2 a.m. with no fallback — an incremental migration gives your team a rollback window'
'Company policy generally favors safer migrations'
'Everyone else on the team also has concerns'
items.explanation: The second version names a cost Sana herself would bear and a benefit she'd personally get — it's framed around her own stakes, not Dev's worry. That's harder to dismiss than an opinion, because it points at something she already has a reason to care about.
items.reference:
Framed around Dev

'I'm worried the hard cutover is risky'

Framed around the listener

'This gives your team a rollback window during your own on-call'

Why: showing someone a reason they already have is stronger than asking them to adopt your worry as their own.
items.learnMore:
Framing around the listener's stakes

The same position can be framed two different ways — and only one of them gives the listener a reason of their own to care.

FramingEffect
Around the asker's worryEasy to dismiss as one person's opinion
Around the listener's own stakesHarder to dismiss because it names something they already have a reason to want

Same underlying position, framed around what the specific listener already cares about, rather than around the asker's concern.

Common mistake

Leading with why the asker is worried, instead of leading with what the listener already stands to gain or lose. The listener's own stakes are almost always the stronger opening.

items.prompt: What's the practical test for whether someone is a real decision-maker, regardless of their formal title?
choices: Whether they attend the decision meeting
Whether the nominal decision-maker would still sign off if that person objected strongly
Whether they have the word 'lead' in their title
Whether they speak first in discussions
items.explanation: The practical test is counterfactual: if this person objected hard, would the decision still go through unchanged? If the answer is no, they're a real decision-maker, regardless of whether their title says so. Attendance, title wording, and who speaks first are all weaker, unreliable signals.
items.reference:
❓ Whose name is on the decision? → the nominal (org-chart) answer
🎯 Whose objection would actually stop it? → the real answer

Why: if the answers differ, effort spent only on the nominal answer doesn't move the real decision.
items.learnMore:
Mapping the real decision network

Two questions separate the org-chart map from the real one, and both need honest answers, not assumed ones.

SignalWhat it suggests
Nominal owner asks 'what do you all think?' before decidingThey're deferring to a real decision-maker
One person's disagreement has reliably delayed past decisionsThat person holds real veto power
A decision moves fast once one person signs offThat person is a bottleneck worth reaching early

Building this map honestly, before doing anything else, is what keeps every later move aimed at the right people.

Common mistake

Assuming the org chart is the real map by default, without checking whether the nominal owner actually exercises independent judgment or consistently defers.

Nothing reliable — it's just a meeting habit

items.prompt: Why does approaching the most-persuadable tech lead first, rather than the hardest holdout, matter beyond just 'starting somewhere easy'?
choices: It doesn't matter — any order works equally well
An early convert becomes a second voice that changes the frame of every later conversation
It's simply less stressful to start with an easy conversation
Persuadable people are more likely to be senior
items.explanation: The order compounds. Once Sana leans a certain way, the next conversation isn't a cold pitch anymore — it includes honest context that a peer already shares the concern, which changes how the next person hears it. That's a structural effect, not just a comfort preference.
items.reference:
TimingEffect
During the meeting, coldPositions default; changing one live feels like losing face
Days before, one-on-oneRoom to genuinely reconsider, arrive already aligned
Weeks before, sequencedEarly converts become messengers for the harder holdouts

Why: the sequencing itself does real work — each earlier conversation changes the frame of the next one.
items.learnMore:
Why timing sequencing matters

It's not just early-versus-late — the order in which people are approached compounds.

Approach orderEffect
Random orderEach conversation starts from zero, no momentum
Most-persuadable firstEarly converts change the frame of later, harder conversations

'Two of your peers already lean this way' is a different opening than a cold pitch — it changes what the third conversation even is.

Common mistake

Treating all coalition conversations as interchangeable and approaching people in a convenient order rather than a strategic one. The order compounds — it isn't just about getting to everyone eventually.

items.prompt: What's the mechanism by which a private, one-on-one conversation days before a decision changes someone's willingness to reconsider, compared to raising the same point live in the meeting?

It removes the audience and the time pressure, giving room to actually think instead of defend a position on the spot
People always agree with whoever speaks to them privately
There is no real mechanism — it's a matter of luck

Privately, days ahead, someone can genuinely reconsider and arrive at the meeting already there — which reads as their own judgment.

items.prompt: Dev reviews Sana's unrelated migration plan for free, a full month before ever mentioning his own concern. Why does this land as a genuine deposit rather than a setup?
choices: Because Dev is naturally a generous person
Because the timing — well before any ask — makes it read as help offered for its own sake, not staged for a future withdrawal
Because he told Sana in advance that it wasn't a setup
Because the favor was large enough to guarantee trust
items.explanation: Timing is what separates a genuine deposit from a performative one. A month of daylight between the favor and the ask makes it read as help offered on its own terms — not staged specifically to set up a future withdrawal, which is what makes a deposit count.
items.reference:
Genuine deposit

Timed well before any ask, unprompted, for its own sake

Performative deposit

Timed right before the ask, easy to read as a setup

Why: getting caught timing a deposit deliberately can subtract from trust rather than simply failing to add to it.
items.learnMore:
Reciprocity: genuine vs. performative, and sizing

Not every favor counts the same, and not every ask is the same size.

Genuine depositPerformative deposit
TimingWell before any ask is nearRight before the ask
Read by the other personReal help, no strings attachedObvious setup, easy to distrust
Effect if discoveredNo effect — it was genuineActively subtracts trust

Sizing matters too: a small favor buys a short, honest conversation — it doesn't automatically buy public support on a large, contested decision.

Common mistake

Offering help in the exact same conversation as the ask, then being surprised the gesture reads as transactional. Genuine deposits need daylight between them and the withdrawal.

items.prompt: If Sana later realized Dev's favor was timed deliberately to set up his ask, what would likely happen to the trust between them?
choices: Nothing — a favor is a favor regardless of timing
It would actively subtract trust, not just fail to add any, because it reveals the asker was thinking about the future withdrawal the whole time
It would have no effect either way since the favor still happened
It would only matter if Sana refused the favor at the time
items.explanation: A discovered performative deposit doesn't just fail to build trust — it actively costs some, because it reveals the gesture was never really about Sana; it was staged for the future ask. That's worse than not helping at all.

The threshold effect

Coalition-building doesn't produce a smooth, proportional payoff for each additional ally — it produces a jump at a specific point.

Allies secured (of 4)What changes

items.explanation: The general principle is narrow and specific, not a blanket rule to always delegate: identify the one piece of the case where your own standing is genuinely thin, and hand off exactly that piece to someone whose standing on that specific question is unquestioned — not the whole argument, and not based on seniority alone.
items.reference:
🗺️ Map who really decides vs. who's nominally listed
⏱️ Build agreement before the moment that counts, in leverage order
🔁 Trade something real, sized to the ask
🎯 Frame around what the listener already wants
🎙️ Hand off the one piece you lack standing on

Why: the same five moves generalize past migrations to any decision someone needs to influence without owning it.
items.learnMore:
Generalizing past this one decision

None of the four (or five, counting the credible-messenger handoff) moves are specific to migrations — they apply to any decision influenced without formal ownership.

This scenarioThe general version
Migration strategy decisionAny decision someone needs to influence without owning it
Tech leads vs. VP FaridWhoever the real decision-makers are vs. whoever's name is on it
Priya's incident dataAny credible messenger closing a specific standing gap

The specific tactics change by context; the underlying four-move structure doesn't.

Common mistake

Treating each of these tactics as a one-off trick for a specific situation, rather than recognizing the same four-move structure recurring across very different decisions.
